Elysium: Simulation-Free Unbalanced Schrödinger Bridges
summary: Reconstructing cellular dynamics from snapshots is challenging because the destructive nature of single-cell measurements makes tracking the same cells over time impossible. Cellular dynamics are inherently stochastic and involve changes in population size through proliferation and apoptosis. Growth-based methods represent population change as a rate on the density, which does not assign exits and entries to individual cells. Unbalanced Schrödinger bridges model individual events, but neural solvers for killed diffusion bridges simulate trajectories during training. We introduce Elysium, a simulation-free solver that jointly learns state transition and mass change. Using a killed Brownian reference and its time reversal, Elysium constructs direct regression objectives from an optimal endpoint coupling and conditional bridge distributions, without simulating trajectories during training. We show that the minimizers of the expected training objectives recover the optimal unbalanced Schrödinger bridge. Empirically, Elysium reconstructs state transitions, population size, and event distributions on simulated benchmarks with known killed-diffusion ground truth, outperforming existing deterministic and bridge-based solvers. On single-cell time courses, it interpolates cell state distributions at unobserved time points, tracks population expansion and contraction, and captures biphasic drug-response dynamics.

Insulin signaling in pericytes is a master regulator of endocrine and vascular niches in pancreatic islets
summary: Insulin plays a crucial role in lowering glycemia, but it is also a powerful anabolic hormone with potent effects on the vasculature. Most studies on insulin vascular actions have focused on endothelial cells. Much less is known about its effects on the mural cells of the microvasculature known as pericytes. This gap in knowledge is particularly relevant for the pancreatic islet microvasculature which is exposed to high insulin levels and relies on local pericytes to efficiently deliver its glucoregulatory hormones. To investigate how insulin affects islet pericyte function and the impact on glucose homeostasis, we generated mice that lack insulin receptors in pericytes (PerIRKO). Loss of insulin signaling in pericytes raised insulin levels, induced islet expansion and beta cell proliferation in the pancreas and in intraocular islet grafts from PerIRKO mice. These changes in beta cell numbers were accompanied by increased islet vascular density, although capillaries were dysfunctional ex vivo, compromising islet hormonal responses to an intravenous glucose challenge. Our study supports that insulin itself regulates islet endocrine and vascular niches through previously unrecognized actions on pericytes, revealing a novel mechanism that links the vasculature to endocrine homeostasis.

title: Endogenous cAMP production within tissue fibroblasts is required for spontaneous fibrosis resolution
summary: Pathologic myofibroblasts (MFs) are pivotal effector cells in the development of persistent tissue fibrosis following parenchymal injury, and their activation and accumulation has been linked to a failure to phenotypically dedifferentiate and thus to resist apoptosis. The second messenger cyclic AMP (cAMP) has been shown to induce MF dedifferentiation and restore their sensitivity to apoptosis in vitro, but its endogenous role within MFs during fibrosis resolution in vivo has not been explored. To test the hypothesis that cAMP generation and signaling within fibroblasts is essential for fibrosis resolution, we leveraged the spontaneously resolving nature of the single-dose intrapulmonary and subcutaneous bleomycin models in mice with an inducible and fibroblast-specific abrogation of cAMP generation owing to deletion of the stimulatory G protein (Gs). Abolishing cAMP generation in fibroblasts after peak lung fibrosis was established led to a failure of the resolution with single-cell RNA seq demonstrating conspicuous differences in pathway enrichment and cellular cross-talk not only in fibroblasts, but also within macrophages and epithelial cells. Spontaneous resolution of skin fibrosis in a model of scleroderma similarly required cAMP production in dermal fibroblasts. We conclude that cAMP generation within fibroblasts after tissue fibrosis has been established is required for its spontaneous resolution in the lung and skin. Our findings provide new insights into factors governing the outcome of tissue fibrosis as well as a mechanistic basis that helps to explain the therapeutic efficacy and ultimate potential of newly available and emerging cAMP-elevating agents.

title: COPS5 maintains spermatogenesis gene expression and piRNA-mediated transposon silencing
summary: COPS5 (CSN5/JAB1), a multifunctional subunit of the COP9 signalosome, is required for male germ cell survival, but how it acts is unclear. We combined a germ cell specific Cops5 conditional knockout (cKO) mouse model with transcriptomic, proteomic and small RNA analysis of P16 testes. Cops5 loss caused progressive spermatogenic arrest after postnatal day 16. At both the mRNA and protein levels, 59 genes were downregulated, including piRNA biogenesis factors such as PIWIL1/MIWI, PIWIL2/MILI, Tudor domain proteins, DDX4, MAEL and MOV10L1. In Cops5 cKO testes, pachytene piRNAs decreased in abundance and diversity, falling from about 56% to 18~30% of total small RNAs, while the 1U bias was retained. Consistent with this, the transposable elements LINE1 and IAP were activated. In human testes, COPS5 was high in spermatogenic cells but reduced by 56.4% in the germ cells of patients with non-obstructive azoospermia (NOA). Thus, COPS5 maintains piRNA homeostasis and transposon silencing, and its loss may contribute to human spermatogenic failure.
